subtype: Approach: seeking advice from a senior mentor [Thinking]
passage: Ganga was unsure how her planning meetings should go. Last Friday's had ended with five people talking and nothing agreed. She asked Sahil sir, the senior manager at the district office, for an hour. On the verandah over tea, he told her to write decisions down as they were made, and to ask each person privately for an estimate before discussing, so the loudest voice would not set the number. "But adapt it," he added. On the bus home Ganga thought aloud, quietly: "My team is shy. They won't say numbers to my face either. But they will write on a slip of paper." On Monday she handed out slips, collected them, and read the numbers out with no names. A quiet clerk's estimate turned out to be the closest.

qa.a: Sahil sir told Ganga to ask each person privately for an estimate.

qa.q: What was Ganga worried about before asking for advice?
qa.a: Ganga was worried and unsure about running planning meetings, since the last one ended with nothing agreed.

qa.q: What else could Ganga try to make meetings work, and why?

qa.q: How might a shy team member see the slips of paper?
qa.a: A shy team member would probably feel relieved and safer, since the number can be shared without saying it face to face.

subtype: Approach: seeking advice from a senior mentor [Thinking]
passage:
Olga had been a project lead at a Warsaw logistics firm for two weeks, and her planning meetings kept falling apart. People talked over each other, nobody remembered what was decided, and the quiet ones gave estimates that were clearly just what the loud ones said.
She thought about it on the tram. I don't know how to run this. Someone must.
So she asked Selin, a senior manager on another floor, for an hour. Over coffee Selin said two things. "Write every decision down in the meeting, on screen, so no one argues later. And ask for estimates privately before the meeting, so people aren't just agreeing."
Olga liked both, but her team was remote on Fridays. So she adapted: a shared document where decisions appear live, and a short form on Thursdays where each person sends an estimate alone.
The next meeting took thirty minutes instead of ninety.

qa.q: How long did the next meeting take?
qa.a: It took thirty minutes instead of ninety.

qa.q: What was Olga thinking on the tram, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She felt unsure and frustrated, admitting she didn't know how to run the meetings and that someone must.

qa.q: What else could Olga do to keep improving the meetings?
qa.a: She could ask the team after a few weeks what is working, so the new format keeps fitting them.

qa.q: How might the quiet team members feel about the private estimates?
qa.a: They may feel more comfortable and respected, able to give honest numbers without being swayed by louder voices.

grounding: Shows a new lead asking a senior manager for advice on running planning meetings, learning to record decisions and gather private estimates, and adapting it.

subtype: Approach: seeking advice from a senior mentor [Thinking]
passage:
The design agency's conference room smelled of coffee and markers. Gopika had just finished another messy planning meeting as a new project lead, and she sat alone afterwards, staring at a whiteboard nobody had written on.
She thought it through. Nobody remembers what we decided. And when I ask for estimates, everyone just repeats whatever Farid says first. I need help.
She sent a message to Neelam, the agency's senior studio manager: "Could you spare an hour this week?"
Neelam could. In her glass cabin she said, "Two things. Write decisions down during the meeting, where everyone sees them. And collect estimates one-on-one beforehand."
Gopika adapted it for her small team. A big sheet on the wall labelled DECISIONS, written in marker during every meeting. And a quick chat with each designer on Monday mornings for their estimates, before Farid could set the number.
By the third meeting, the estimates were all different, and much closer to reality.

qa.q: Whose estimate did everyone repeat before the change?
qa.a: Everyone repeated whatever Farid said first.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel sitting alone after the meeting?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and unsure, staring at the empty whiteboard and deciding she needed help.

qa.q: What else could Gopika do if Farid still dominates meetings?
qa.a: She could invite quieter designers to share their estimate first during the meeting too, so different views are heard.

qa.q: How might Farid see the new Monday chats?
qa.a: Farid might be surprised that his number no longer sets the pace, though he may also appreciate more accurate plans.

grounding: Shows a new lead asking a senior manager for advice on planning meetings, learning to record decisions and gather estimates privately, and adapting it.
